news.title: Steve Witkoff's grandson born on 15th anniversary of son Andrew's death
news.text: Alex Witkoff, son of US President Donald Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, marked the 15th anniversary of his brother Andrew's death on Saturday by sharing that his newborn nephew was born on the same date and named in Andrew's memory, a coincidence he described as "bashert," or "meant to be.""Exactly 15 years ago, we unexpectedly lost my beloved brother Andrew," Witkoff wrote, reflecting on his brother's death. On the anniversary of Andrew's death, the family welcomed a new life when his brother Zach Witkoff and Zach's wife, Sophie, had a son named Theodore Andrew in memory of his late uncle.'In Judaism, we call this "bashert"' The timing carried particular significance because that day was the only one on which the couple's doctor was available to deliver the baby. "In Judaism, we call this 'bashert,' meant to be," Witkoff wrote.For the Witkoff family, a day long associated with tragedy has now taken on new meaning. "A day forever marked by unimaginable loss now carries with it new life, joy, and hope. Theodore will carry forward Andrew's name, memory, and spirit," Witkoff wrote.Fifteen years ago today, we unexpectedly lost my beloved brother Andrew.Today, my brother @ZachWitkoff and Sophi welcomed their son, Theodore Andrew, into the world. Of all days, today was the only day their doctor could deliver him.In Judaism, we call that beshert - meant to…— Alex Witkoff (@Alex_Witkoff) August 15, 2026Andrew Witkoff died of an opioid overdose in 2011 at age 22. Steve Witkoff previously spoke about the loss at a conference on the opioid epidemic organized by First Lady Melania Trump."After my son died, I found myself clinging to his memory, even his possessions. His student ID is in my pocket now, I have worn his ring since he died, I came here today wearing his watch, I kept his guitar, and I thought I would keep it forever, but I gave it to a dear friend of mine, a dear friend of Andrew's, and a music fan like him, Donald Trump," he said.Today, Sophi and I welcomed our son, Theodore Andrew Witkoff, into the world. He was born 15 years to the day after I lost my beloved brother, Andrew. A day of profound joy, love, and remembrance. Theodore will carry his uncle's name and legacy with him always.— Zach Witkoff (@ZachWitkoff) August 14, 2026Steve Witkoff's first grandson named after Donald TrumpTheodore is Steve Witkoff's second grandchild; the first is nearly-two-year-old Don James Witkoff, born to Zach Witkoff in December 2024. He is named after Donald Trump, a fact that both Trump and Witkoff publicized online shortly after Don's birth. "Congratulations to Zach and Sophi Witkoff on the birth of their son, Don James Witkoff (DJW), named after me (Thank you!). I wish them the best today, the day of DJW's Bris," Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time. "Don will have a great, beautiful, and successful life. This will be, because of him, a very important date as the years go by!"Thank you Mr. President @realDonaldTrump. It is an honor to name our son after the greatest President of all time and all that you stand for . https://t.co/K5eg7bhujl— Zach Witkoff (@ZachWitkoff) December 15, 2024 "Thank you Mr. President," Zach Witkoff wrote in a response on Twitter/X. "It is an honor to name our son after the greatest President of all time and all that you stand for."Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

news.title: 'Mr. President, he is winning': Netanyahu aide told Trump despite weak polls - report
news.text: When Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump met in the Oval Office on July 28, Trump asked Netanyahu how he was doing in the polls ahead of the October 27 Knesset election, according to a Friday Axios report.Netanyahu paused, the report noted. Then one of his advisers piped up: "Mr. President, he is winning," the aide said, according to Axios, citing a US official familiar with the exchange.At the time of the meeting, the coalition bloc had 49 predicted Knesset seats, according to a Maariv poll - 12 short of the 62 seats needed for a majority. A more recent poll conducted on Friday predicted 48 seats. Ahead of the meeting, Netanyahu hoped to secure Trump's support for his reelection campaign ahead of the October 27 election, people familiar with the matter said.For months before the meeting, Trump publicly stated that he had urged Netanyahu not to launch further strikes in Lebanon and that he wanted to see Israel withdraw from parts of Syria. On several occasions, he had suggested that Washington and Jerusalem do not necessarily see eye-to-eye on every regional issue.The US president recently said that "Bibi is his own worst enemy," according to Axios, citing two people who spoke with Trump about Netanyahu.Netanyahu uses Likud's first reserved slot for businessman who called Trump 'piece of s***'Likud announced on Monday that entrepreneur and businessman Oren Dobronsky, a co-founder of the tech company Hotbar who spent years working in Silicon Valley, would receive Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's first reserved slot on the party's Knesset list ahead of the elections.Shortly after the announcement of his reserved slot, it emerged that Dobronsky had previously attacked US President Donald Trump, calling him “a morally corrupt person” in a post on X/Twitter.Dobronsky walks back statement following backlash over Trump commentsHowever, on Monday, Dobronsky walked back his statement. He wrote on Facebook that “President Trump is the greatest friend that Israel ever had in the Whitehouse [sic]. I posted in his favor countless times. On one occasion, not knowing all the facts, I lost my temper and posted something I regret. My apologies to President Trump, whom I admire deerly [sic].”Dobronsky is well-known in the Israeli and American tech industries. He co-founded a company that developed a toolbar for Internet browsers and later completed a significant exit. He subsequently continued working as an entrepreneur and invested in start-ups.Idan Kweller, Moshe Cohen, Keshet Neev, and James Genn contributed to this report.

news.title: Colombia’s President asks Trump to suspend tariffs as earthquake strains economy
news.text:
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella on Saturday asked US President Donald Trump to temporarily suspend tariffs on Colombian products, saying the move would help businesses cope with the economic impact of a deadly earthquake.
US tariffs on Colombian goods increased from 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent in late July, with some exceptions, including coffee and oil.
“I asked him to consider to temporarily suspend the high tariffs that are affecting Colombian products, in order to give some relief to our business owners, who are facing very difficult times due to the effects of the earthquake,” De la Espriella said on X.
The higher tariffs took effect on July 24, replacing a global duty introduced by Trump earlier this year that was due to expire.
Trump offers condolences after earthquake
De la Espriella said he spoke with Trump for around 10 minutes and that the US president expressed his condolences over deaths caused by Monday’s 7.4-magnitude earthquake.
“The conversation was very friendly and cordial,” the Colombian leader said.
“I told him that we have a huge challenge ahead: rebuilding Colombia amid the extremely difficult and apocalyptic economic situation that I inherited.”
The earthquake devastated the western Colombian cities of Cali and Pereira, killing nearly 300 people and destroying almost 13,000 homes.
De la Espriella strengthens US ties
Trump endorsed De la Espriella, a millionaire lawyer-turned-politician, during his presidential campaign.
After taking office, De la Espriella, who succeeded leftist Gustavo Petro, joined the so-called “Shield of the Americas”, an anti-cartel alliance led by Trump and comprising pro-US governments across Latin America, including Argentina, Ecuador and El Salvador.
The member countries exchange information and coordinate judicial and security forces to tackle transnational criminal activity.
De la Espriella also plans to establish a military alliance with the United States and Israel to strengthen his campaign against guerrillas.
(With agency inputs)

news.title: Hamas leader heads to Cairo for Gaza talks ahead of Kushner visit
news.text:
Hamas political leader and chief negotiator Khalil al-Hayya is set to travel to Cairo for talks with Egyptian officials, a Hamas source has told the AFP news agency, ahead of a planned Middle East visit by US President Donald Trump’s envoy, Jared Kushner.

In his first visit to the country since taking over Hamas’s leadership in late July, al-Hayya is expected to meet Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad on Sunday morning, according to the source.

Next week, Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, will travel to Israel and Egypt in an effort to narrow differences over a Gaza plan that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected. Kushner is set to be accompanied by Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative for Gaza.

The trip follows Netanyahu’s public dismissal of a 15-point plan under which Hamas had agreed to hand its weapons to a new Palestinian governing committee.

“We continue to await pressure from the mediators and the US side on Netanyahu and his government to compel him to abide by the roadmap,” Hamas political bureau member Basem Naim told AFP on Friday.

Meanwhile, Israeli attacks have continued in Gaza.

On Saturday, Israeli fire killed two Palestinians and wounded 14 others after the military carried out air strikes, artillery shelling and demolitions in different parts of the strip, according to the territory’s Ministry of Health.

More than 1,250 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed by Israeli fire since the ceasefire took effect in October last year, according to Palestinian official sources, with the overall death toll since October 2023 exceeding 73,300.

Netanyahu formally rejected the Board of Peace plan last Sunday, saying Israeli forces “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed”.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said this week that troops would also remain in occupied “security zones” in Lebanon and Syria, declaring there will be a continued Israeli military presence across all three fronts.
news.summary: Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya to meet Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad in Cairo amid ongoing Gaza tensions.

news.title: Colombia asks Trump to suspend tariffs as country reels from earthquake  - Guyana Inquirer – Daily Guyana News
news.text:
Colombia’s new president has called on United States President Donald Trump to suspend tariffs targeting the South American country, which is reeling from a deadly earthquake that has killed hundreds.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Saturday that he had requested the US “temporarily suspend” tariffs on Colombia to give “relief” to business owners.

On Monday, a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia, killing at least 294 people and damaging or destroying tens of thousands of buildings across the country, according to Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management.

US tariffs on Colombian products rose from 10 percent to 12.5 percent in late July, with a few exceptions including coffee and oil. The US is Colombia’s top export market.

The Colombian leader described his 10-minute conversation with President Trump as “very friendly and cordial”.

“I told him that we have a huge challenge ahead: rebuilding Colombia amid the extremely difficult and apocalyptic economic situation that I inherited,” de la Espriella said.

Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately $6.4bn needed for reconstruction, local media have reported.

Shortly after a legal defeat on “Liberation Day” tariffs, the White House announced renewed tariffs targeting nearly every US trading partner, including Colombia, based on what it said were failures to uphold anti-forced labour measures.

Trump endorsed the right-wing de la Espriella, a millionaire lawyer-turned-politician, during his run for the presidency that culminated in a close victory over leftist Ivan Cepeda in June.

Since taking office in early August, de la Espriella has joined the so-called “Shield of the Americas”, an anti-cartel alliance headed by Trump and involving multiple South American nations.

The new Colombian president has also said he plans to forge a military alliance with the US and Israel to help bolster the country’s long-running conflict with armed groups.

news.title: At least five reported dead amid flooding in US state of Indiana  - Guyana Inquirer – Daily Guyana News
news.text:
Authorities in the Midwestern United States have reported at least five deaths in Indiana after the state was struck with fierce storms and flooding.

Rescue workers continue to seek out those stranded by the storms, which drenched Indiana over the past week.

Governor Mike Braun had called for a presidential emergency declaration on Friday, in order to access greater resources for the state.

On Saturday, he issued a public statement announcing that the federal government had pledged assistance.

“I spoke with President [Donald] Trump today about the severe storms and historic flooding impacting Indiana, and he informed me that he intends to approve our request for a Presidential Emergency Declaration,” Braun, a Republican, wrote in a social media post.

“I’m grateful to President Trump for his commitment to getting Hoosiers the federal assistance we need as we continue responding and recovering.”

Emergency workers have used boats to rescue people from homes inundated by rising waters.

The White River in Indianapolis, Indiana, was among the waterways that overflowed its banks over the last week, causing dangerous flooding.

Indianapolis Mayor Joe Hogsett said that the area is experiencing its worst flooding in more than 30 years. The National Weather Service has reported that more than 280mm (11 inches) of rain fell over two days in some areas.

Sheriff deputies in Delaware County said on Friday that they had found the body of a deceased 58-year-old woman, whom they believe died trying to drive her vehicle through floodwaters.

Authorities caution against attempting to cross flooded areas in a car, warning that vehicles can become stranded.

A four-year-old child also died after a tree fell on a home in Jennings County this week, and law enforcement found the body of a teen who was reported missing on Wednesday after jumping into a river.

“My heart is with the families and loved ones of the five Hoosiers we have lost and every family whose life has been changed by these storms,” Braun said on Saturday. “Please continue to take flooding seriously and stay away from floodwaters.”

news.title: BBC tries to force Donald Trump's family to testify over £7billion defamation lawsuit
news.text:
The BBC has attempted to subpoena members of Donald Trump’s family to defend itself from the £7.4 billion defamation lawsuit issued by the US President.

The broadcaster is seeking subpoenas to force Mr Trump’s eldest son Donald Jr, his daughter Ivanka and his son-in-law Jared Kushner to testify in the case, which revolves around whether the President’s actions fuelled the January 6, 2021 storming of the US Capitol.

Lawyers for the BBC said the Trump family members ‘without question have personal knowledge’ about his behaviour leading up to the attack.

Mr Trump is suing the BBC over a 2024 Panorama documentary which claimed he gave a speech in Washington DC that allegedly incited rioters to storm the building.

The President claims that the show ‘spliced together’ different parts of his speech to make it appear he was endorsing violence.

He accused the BBC of ‘intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring’ the speech.

The BBC has apologised for the editing saying ‘it gave the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action’ but denied its actions were grounds for a lawsuit.

It has asked a judge to dismiss the case. Donald Jr and Ivanka were present as their father gave the speech and Ivanka’s husband, Mr Kushner, drafted a proposed statement for Mr Trump to broadcast during the riot to condemn the violence.

Court filings show the BBC tried to serve subpoenas to the Kushners at their Miami home in May but were blocked by the Secret Service. An attempt to serve Donald Jr at Trump Tower in New York was also unsuccessful.

In a motion filed in Miami Federal Court on Friday, the BBC asked the judge to authorise service by mail or email.

Lawyers for the Trump family declined to comment.

The case is set to go to trial in February next year.
news.summary: The broadcaster is seeking subpoenas to force Mr Trump's eldest son Donald Jr, his daughter Ivanka and his son-in-law Jared Kushner to testify in the case.

news.title: Turkish President signals expansion of Mecca Defence Pact, says Egypt could join
news.text:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has opened the door to Egypt joining the defence agreement that Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed last week, saying Cairo could become part of the expanding arrangement.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Erdogan described Egypt’s participation as “possible” and said the agreement could accommodate additional members.
“This agreement has sent an important message to the world,” Erdogan said, referring to the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
What the Mecca pact means
Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the Mecca Pact on August 7. The agreement commits the three countries to treat an armed attack on one member as an attack on all three.
Turkiye’s defence ministry said the three countries would step up military coordination under the agreement. The plans include meetings between defence and foreign ministers and military chiefs, along with joint exercises involving land, naval and air forces.
The countries also plan exercises involving air defence and unmanned systems, while their defence industries will work more closely on technology, production and logistics.
“Under the accord, strategic political ​and military mechanisms plan to be established involving the Defence Ministers, Foreign Ministers, ​and Chiefs of General Staff/Armed Forces Commanders, and that coordination among the three countries will ‌be conducted ⁠at the highest level,” the ministry said.
The ministry added, “The aim is to provide not ​only product and system ​supply, but also ⁠joint development and production, technology cooperation, and sustainable maintenance and logistics support.”
It said the partnership would prioritise unmanned and autonomous systems, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence capabilities.
The arrangement has drawn comparisons with Nato's Article 5 collective defence clause. However, Pakistani officials have stressed that the pact does not amount to a Nati equivalent and does not target any particular country.
Ankara focuses on wider regional security
Turkiye also joined discussions in Jeddah aimed at creating an international coalition to protect Red Sea shipping.
Erdogan meanwhile addressed tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, as well as the conflicts in Syria, Gaza and Lebanon. He said Ankara wanted the strait reopened, arguing that its continued closure served no one’s interests.
He credited Qatar with an important role in efforts to mediate an end to regional fighting and said Turkiye would continue supporting its neighbours through the ongoing turmoil.
Erdogan speaks on Syria, Gaza and Lebanon
On Syria, Erdogan said Ankara would do everything possible to support stability and confirmed plans to visit the country. He said Syria’s Kurds would have “a share of peace and stability” and added that Turkiye would continue strengthening ties with Kurdish communities while safeguarding their rights across the region.
Turning to Gaza, Erdogan said Turkiye “cannot leave Gaza alone” and would continue doing whatever was necessary to support it. He said Hamas was meeting its commitments in good faith while Israel continued its war.
On Lebanon, Erdogan described continued Israeli attacks as a serious concern for Ankara. He said he raised the need to end the war in Lebanon with US President Donald Trump during Trump’s recent visit to Turkiye and stressed Washington’s role in ending the fighting.

news.title: Trump flaunts an article that credits Biden for lower drug prices and not him
news.text:
US President Donald Trump was spotted on Saturday flaunting the recent Washington Post article about reduced drug prices that suggested that it is former President Joe Biden who deserves the credit, not him. The White House flooded social media with the photograph of Trump showing off the article with the headline "Prescription drug prices record sharpest drop in more than 60 years”.
However, they failed to mention that the expert cited in the article actually credited Biden for the price drop, not the current US President. On its official accounts, the White House triumphantly captioned the photograph of Trump: “POV: you bring the receipts.” Karoline Leavitt, the outgoing White House press secretary, also shared the post.
The image was one of several taken during one of Trump's staged photo-ops on Friday, when he approached reporters with a copy of the headline. Holding up a printout of the headline and the first five lines of the article, the president waved the page around and encouraged the press pool to record and photograph it. “The headline today is exactly that,” he said proudly. “Did you see it?”
He went on to read the good news aloud and remarked: "OK, got it? Everybody have it?” he asked. “I told you that was going to happen.” Before stepping away, Trump repeated the headline. “Prescription drug prices down more than at any time over 60 years,” he said. “What else do I have to say?"
What the article was actually about
However, what the president did not mention was the actual text of the article that was published by The Washington Post on Thursday. The American news outlet reported that while the Trump White House “took credit for” the biggest year-over-year drop in drug prices in more than 60 years in July, independent experts “said a Biden-era policy that requires Medicare to negotiate prices for some popular prescription drugs is more likely to be driving down costs”.
“The Inflation Reduction Act was a signature accomplishment of former president Joe Biden, a sprawling measure enacted in 2022 that aimed to lower prescription drug prices by requiring Medicare, the federal health program for the elderly, to begin negotiating the prices it pays drugmakers for an array of popular and costly prescription drugs,” the article read. “The first price reductions took effect at the beginning of this year.”
According to the Consumer Price Index data, the price of the prescription drugs fell by 3.1 per cent in July. It is pertinent to note that the index was released by the Bureau of Labour Statistics, whose former head was fired by Trump last year over weaker-than-expected job numbers he called “fake”.
The Washington Post went ahead and quoted Richard Frank, a professor emeritus of health economics at Harvard University, expressing doubt that Trump’s policies were behind the drop in drug prices. “If I was a betting guy on what mattered most, it would be probably stuff around the Inflation Reduction Act,” Frank said, adding that Trump’s efforts “wouldn’t be where I’d place my money”.
Meanwhile, another expert, Stacie Dusetzina, a health policy professor at Vanderbilt University, told the Post the law signed by Biden was a more likely explanation for the decline in prices than any of Trump’s initiatives. Despite this, Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, posted a screenshot of the Post’s headline on his X account on Thursday with no link to the article. “All thanks to President Trump!” Cheung wrote.

news.title: For the Left, When Outrage Becomes Instinct, Facts Are Optional
news.text:
Repair the Reflecting Pool? Outrage. Build a new White House ballroom? Lawsuits. Follow Secret Service guidance to avoid a possible assassination attempt? Mockery, apparently, if you're Trump.

This week, Trump confirmed that the Secret Service and the military secretly swapped his plane when he left the NATO summit in Turkey last month because of a possible security threat. He hid in a catering truck before boarding a separate, secret jet out of the country. The traveling press corps stayed on the original plane with no idea any of it was happening, and once they found out, they were furious that Trump's team had used them as decoys.

Cartoonists and pundits on the left responded with mockery instead of any acknowledgment that the president of the United States had just dodged another possible attempt on his life.

Trump has already survived multiple assassination attempts, including one that left him with a bullet wound to the ear. The Iranian government has made no secret of wanting him dead. Nothing about that seems to register with a press corps that cares more about a classified security decision leaving them out of the loop than about their subject making it out alive.

I get a front-row seat to how the Left processes stories like this. I'm the writer half of Margolis & Cox, a nationally syndicated editorial cartoon duo, and the syndicate we work with leans left, which means I see the competition's cartoons a lot. In the days after the plane swap became public, plenty of them piled on, drawing Trump as a chicken and mocking a man who has survived multiple assassination attempts for following his own protective detail's advice.

Look, I get criticizing policies you don’t like, and even trying to make character an issue. But not everything deserves a pile-on. Certainly, this didn’t.

ICYMI: It's Official, Democrats Want to Abolish ICE

Even Bill Maher, no one's idea of a Trump defender, wasn't buying the outrage. Discussing the incident with his panel on his HBO show, Maher laid out exactly what happened. "President Trump foiled the assassins again this week," Maher said. "He jumped on the plane that wasn't the plane, but he left everybody else on the other plane. If the Iranians were going to shoot down that plane, goodbye, Marco Rubio and a lot of other people. No, I'm not judging here. I'm sure that's what the Secret Service told him to do."

Maher then posed the real question, asking whether a president of either party would have handled it differently. "My question is, because I've heard it is the president's discretion whether he could do that or not, do you think any other president would have done it differently?" he asked, naming Jimmy Carter, Barack Obama, and Ronald Reagan as examples. "Like, say, Jimmy Carter. He was like Mr. Christian Guy. Would he have left his friends on that other plane? What about Obama? What about Reagan?"

Panelist Kristen Soltis Anderson didn't hesitate. "Donald Trump has had a number of credible threats on his life, traced back to the Iranian government," she said. "He got his ear shot. So I kind of think if you're Donald Trump, you do what the Secret Service tells you." Maher agreed. "Yeah, I would," he said.

Former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo backed her up. "I think they all would," he said. Maher pressed him on it. "You think they all would?" he asked. Cuomo held his ground. "Yeah, I think they would do what the Secret Service said to do," he said. "Yes, it's his decision, but you rarely go against what the Secret Service is advising."

It’s getting tiring at this point, don’t you think?

news.title: Colombia asks Trump to suspend tariffs as country reels from earthquake  | Barbados Gazette – Barbados &
news.text:
Colombia’s new president has called on United States President Donald Trump to suspend tariffs targeting the South American country, which is reeling from a deadly earthquake that has killed hundreds.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Saturday that he had requested the US “temporarily suspend” tariffs on Colombia to give “relief” to business owners.

On Monday, a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia, killing at least 294 people and damaging or destroying tens of thousands of buildings across the country, according to Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management.

US tariffs on Colombian products rose from 10 percent to 12.5 percent in late July, with a few exceptions including coffee and oil. The US is Colombia’s top export market.

The Colombian leader described his 10-minute conversation with President Trump as “very friendly and cordial”.

“I told him that we have a huge challenge ahead: rebuilding Colombia amid the extremely difficult and apocalyptic economic situation that I inherited,” de la Espriella said.

Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately $6.4bn needed for reconstruction, local media have reported.

Shortly after a legal defeat on “Liberation Day” tariffs, the White House announced renewed tariffs targeting nearly every US trading partner, including Colombia, based on what it said were failures to uphold anti-forced labour measures.

Trump endorsed the right-wing de la Espriella, a millionaire lawyer-turned-politician, during his run for the presidency that culminated in a close victory over leftist Ivan Cepeda in June.

Since taking office in early August, de la Espriella has joined the so-called “Shield of the Americas”, an anti-cartel alliance headed by Trump and involving multiple South American nations.

The new Colombian president has also said he plans to forge a military alliance with the US and Israel to help bolster the country’s long-running conflict with armed groups.

news.title: At least five reported dead amid flooding in US state of Indiana  | Barbados Gazette – Barbados &
news.text:
Authorities in the Midwestern United States have reported at least five deaths in Indiana after the state was struck with fierce storms and flooding.

Rescue workers continue to seek out those stranded by the storms, which drenched Indiana over the past week.

Governor Mike Braun had called for a presidential emergency declaration on Friday, in order to access greater resources for the state.

On Saturday, he issued a public statement announcing that the federal government had pledged assistance.

“I spoke with President [Donald] Trump today about the severe storms and historic flooding impacting Indiana, and he informed me that he intends to approve our request for a Presidential Emergency Declaration,” Braun, a Republican, wrote in a social media post.

“I’m grateful to President Trump for his commitment to getting Hoosiers the federal assistance we need as we continue responding and recovering.”

Emergency workers have used boats to rescue people from homes inundated by rising waters.

The White River in Indianapolis, Indiana, was among the waterways that overflowed its banks over the last week, causing dangerous flooding.

Indianapolis Mayor Joe Hogsett said that the area is experiencing its worst flooding in more than 30 years. The National Weather Service has reported that more than 280mm (11 inches) of rain fell over two days in some areas.

Sheriff deputies in Delaware County said on Friday that they had found the body of a deceased 58-year-old woman, whom they believe died trying to drive her vehicle through floodwaters.

Authorities caution against attempting to cross flooded areas in a car, warning that vehicles can become stranded.

A four-year-old child also died after a tree fell on a home in Jennings County this week, and law enforcement found the body of a teen who was reported missing on Wednesday after jumping into a river.

“My heart is with the families and loved ones of the five Hoosiers we have lost and every family whose life has been changed by these storms,” Braun said on Saturday. “Please continue to take flooding seriously and stay away from floodwaters.”

Trump endorsed the right-wing de la Espriella, a millionaire lawyer-turned-politician, during his run for the presidency that culminated in a close victory over leftist Ivan Cepeda in June.

Since taking office in early August, de la Espriella has joined the so-called “Shield of the Americas”, an anti-cartel alliance headed by Trump and involving multiple South American nations.

Authorities in the Midwestern United States have reported at least five deaths in Indiana after the state was struck with fierce storms and flooding.

Rescue workers continue to seek out those stranded by the storms, which drenched Indiana over the past week.

Emergency workers have used boats to rescue people from homes inundated by rising waters.

The White River in Indianapolis, Indiana, was among the waterways that overflowed its banks over the last week, causing dangerous flooding.

Indianapolis Mayor Joe Hogsett said that the area is experiencing its worst flooding in more than 30 years. The National Weather Service has reported that more than 280mm (11 inches) of rain fell over two days in some areas.

Sheriff deputies in Delaware County said on Friday that they had found the body of a deceased 58-year-old woman, whom they believe died trying to drive her vehicle through floodwaters.

Authorities caution against attempting to cross flooded areas in a car, warning that vehicles can become stranded.

news.title: Push to oust US ambassador from Canada expands - and ‘51st state’ could take up the issue in fall
news.text:
More than 170,000 Canadians have signed a petition demanding the removal of U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, after months of boycotting American goods and canceling trips in response to escalating trade disputes and talk of annexing the country.

Submitted on July 21 by a Calgary resident, the parliamentary petition urges the Canadian government to declare Hoekstra persona non grata under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. It also calls for a parliamentary committee to investigate “U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs.”

Under Canadian parliamentary rules, online petitions require only 500 validated signatures to earn a formal presentation on the floor of the House of Commons. 

Because this filing far exceeded that threshold, Green Party Leader Elizabeth May is expected to bring the matter forward for parliamentary debate when lawmakers return this fall, The New York Times reported. Once presented, the federal government is required to lay a formal response on the table within 45 calendar days.

The petition follows a decline in relations between the two countries. A Pew survey released in June indicated that 35 percent of Canadians viewed the United States as a reliable partner, down from 82 percent in 2022. Canadian leisure travel to the U.S. has dropped by more than a quarter over the last year, while Canadian consumers have increasingly turned away from American products.

Tensions have been high between the U.S. and its neighbor since President Donald Trump returned to office. He blasted the country and its trade with the U.S., threatened new tariffs and even talked about Canada becoming the “51st state.”

“If people wanted to play the game right, it would be 100 percent certain that they’d become a state,” Trump said early in his term.

After the U.S. administration imposed fresh tariffs on Canadian goods, Prime Minister Mark Carney warned at the World Economic Forum in January that global alliances faced “a rupture, not a transition.”

Tensions escalated further over Canadian objections to U.S. rhetoric regarding Greenland, as well as an Ontario-funded advertising campaign against tariffs that quoted former President Ronald Reagan.

Military cooperation has also faced strain. Following discussions regarding Canada’s procurement of American F-35 fighter jets, Hoekstra warned that changes to Ottawa’s purchase plans could affect North American Aerospace Defense Command operations.

“NORAD would have to be altered,” Hoekstra told CBC News. 

The petition accuses Hoekstra, a former Republican representative from Michigan and former ambassador to the Netherlands, of harming bilateral relations and normalizing rhetoric regarding the annexation of Canada as a “51st state.” The petition also highlights social media posts by the ambassador referencing these annexation remarks, as well as statements dismissing Canadian public concern as “emotional.”

The filing also alleges that Hoekstra engaged in improper political involvement by meeting with Alberta separatists, raising questions regarding U.S. positions on Canadian unity. The petition further cites his acquaintance with the developer of a voter ID application used by Alberta separatist groups. Hoekstra has denied allegations of improper engagement with separatist entities.

Despite the controversy, representatives from the cross-border business community have defended Hoekstra's work. Rick Tachuk, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Canada, stated that Hoekstra remained accessible to business leaders and focused on trade relations, The New York Times reported.

“He at times can be blunt, but, in many respects, that is an advantage for us because he helps articulate the view of the president, and helps us understand what the challenges are,” Tachuk said. 

No U.S. ambassador has ever been declared persona non grata by Canada, though foreign envoys have been expelled globally during historical diplomatic crises. 

Canadian officials have not formally summoned Hoekstra, but other U.S. envoys in Europe — including those to France and Belgium — have recently been called in by host governments over comments about local affairs.
news.summary: Pew research shows only 35 percent of Canadians view the US as a reliable partner

news.title: Nigeria’s most urgent health issue
news.text:
The most urgent and topical health issue currently ravaging developing countries is the rise of malaria resurgence, driven by climate change, weakened health systems, conflict, and reduced international aid. All these factors are prevalent in the Nigerian environment.

Reduced international aid via the likes of the United States Agency for International Development, and the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, have negatively impacted how various governments in sub-Saharan Africa, in particular, are able to respond to these diseases.

In the case of these two United States government agencies, outright cancellation of their funding by the Donald Trump administration has been hard-hitting. It has screwed healthcare budgets throughout the region, and Nigeria has not been spared.

In less than two years since the funds were cut off, there has been a resurgence of new AIDS cases around the country. Malaria, never fully controlled but probably contained with some success, is also staging a comeback.

In East and Southern Africa, the effects of climate change have enabled an increase in malaria transmission by as much as 84 per cent and 91 per cent respectively in both regions, according to a recent study published in the journal Nature.

Malaria cases have increased globally by 8.5 per cent since 2015, reversing earlier gains and pushing many high‑burden developing countries further from global targets. This resurgence is happening alongside other major pressures such as tuberculosis, maternal mortality, and health‑system disruptions, but malaria stands out because it is rapidly worsening, climate‑sensitive, and disproportionately affects the poorest populations.

Malaria is a mosquito‑borne parasitic disease caused mainly by Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. It spreads through the female Anopheles mosquito, which thrives in warm, humid environments, and most favourably at temperatures around 25°C.

These conditions are increasingly common due to climate change. Other less common variants of Plasmodium responsible for this disease are Plasmodium ovale, Plasmodium malariae and Plasmodium knowlesi. Therefore, there is a huge belt of geographical space between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn that stretches from Latin America across the African continent to East Asia where various species of this parasite are actively causing disease.

What malaria is and why it is resurging is also helped by the development of resistance strains of the parasite and those whose composition has been altered by the use of substandard medications against the disease.

In many parts of sub-Saharan Africa, where the local populations often developed some innate immunity against the disease, such protection appears to have been lost due to socio-economic factors that have to do with economic migration and violent conflict. Malaria is a severe threat to Nigeria due to a deadly combination of scale, vulnerability, and systemic challenges.

Despite recent progress, the numbers are stark: in 2024, the year in which the most recent figures are available, Nigeria accounted for an estimated 24.3 per cent of global malaria cases and 30.3 per cent of all malaria deaths. We shall examine here why malaria is such a critical issue.

It is associated with a massive human toll, which in sheer numbers means that nearly 200,000 malaria-related deaths occurred in Nigeria in 2024, representing nearly 40 per cent of global malaria deaths among children under five. The most vulnerable groups are children and pregnant women because they bear the brunt of this impact.

Beyond the stark statistics in the toll of human loss, this disease bears the hallmarks of a crippling economic burden. Nigeria faces the highest economic burden of malaria in West Africa, costing nearly $11bn (US) annually. This includes massive productivity losses such as up to 30 per cent of workdays lost in agriculture, school absenteeism, and high household treatment costs, over N1,112 monthly per household.

Then, there is the drug resistance threat, which has become a huge problem characterised by treatment failures with the emergence of partial resistance to Artemisinin, a plant extract native to South East Asia that has, in the last three decades, formed the core of front-line treatments. This is a looming crisis.

While mutations are still under investigation, the risk of treatment failure is real, demanding urgent policy changes like diversifying first-line therapies. In East Africa, several countries have reverted to the use of the old medication, Chloroquine, as a first-line drug in the treatment of this formidable disease. Still, systemic gaps persist.

Healthcare challenges persist, including a situation in which nearly two-thirds of treatment funding comes from households as out-of-pocket expenses. In addition, misdiagnosis issues, such as low accuracy in diagnosis that comes out of poorly manned private laboratories, and inconsistent application of treatment guidelines continue to erode any progress made in combating the disease.

While Nigeria has halved its prevalence since 2010, from 42 per cent to about 15 per cent by introducing vaccines and preventive treatments, these new threats make sustained and innovative action critical. First of all, the whole society has to be actively involved in efforts to control this disease and ultimately defeat it. That may be a tall order, but a viable plan developed with the active participation of the populace is a good point to start from.

To address its massive malaria burden, Nigeria has launched an ambitious, multi-layered strategy targeting a reduction by half in prevalence and mortality by 2030. The approach combines aggressive prevention with a new focus on tackling drug resistance. Basically, the plan aims to scale up targeted prevention by aggressively distributing insecticide-treated nets to 11 states using the available manpower in the various local governments.

However, as a personal witness to this laudable scheme, workers from the local governments have done the neighbourhood rounds at intervals and taken the required census only to not turn up again to deliver the nets. So that unless these efforts have some way of being monitored, it will end up like so many other laudable plans developed in the healthcare sector.

Seasonal malaria chemoprevention, which targets some 29 million children in 21 states, is another effort being made by the federal government to expand prevention. The rollout of the malaria vaccine is another chink in the armour already said to be protecting more than 700,000 children. 

Environmental control efforts to deal with the mosquito larvae at their breeding spaces are another new initiative. It is called Larval Source Management, and it aims to destroy mosquito breeding sites in six states including Lagos and Rivers, alongside next-generation ITNs to counter insecticide resistance.

Since Artemisinin resistance is a looming threat, experts urge Nigeria to adopt Multiple First-Line Therapies using different Artemisinin combination therapies to reduce the selection pressure on the parasite.

From the various research labs and clinical application of available treatments, it will help to scale up molecular and genomic surveillance to track resistance mutations in real time and inform rapid policy changes. This will ensure a shift from a one-size-fits-all approach to tailoring interventions by state.

Questions and answers

Sunday Doctor, thank you for the wonderful and charitable work you have been doing for us over the years through Sunday PUNCH. May Almighty God continue to protect, guide and guard you always. My daughter is 18 years old, and she regularly develops boils in her armpits. We have taken her to different hospitals for treatment, and although they go away after taking antibiotics, they always come back. What can she use to treat them? 0802*******

Thank you very much for your kind words and prayers. Your daughter may have these boils in close relation to her periods, in which case, no antibiotic treatment is needed. You should verify this connection with her, and if that is the case and the boils do not cause any significant pain or fever, they will resolve on their own.

 Sunday Doctor, please, I have eczema on my face. I have been using Ketoconazole cream recommended by a doctor, but it is not working. What should I do? 081*******

There are a few problems with that. You did not state how long you used the cream for and at what frequency. These are important yardsticks, but if a doctor recommended it, we shall assume that you have used it correctly. The problem then could be whether it is eczema you are treating. A correct diagnosis is vital to getting the proper treatment. So, you either go back to that doctor or go to a hospital for a proper examination.

 Sunday Doctor, I was recently given a worm expeller to give to my one-year-old son when I took him for immunisation. Should I go ahead and use it? 070*******

Well, routine deworming exercises can start as early as 1 year with a doctor’s guidance in places where worm infestation is endemic. However, it is generally advised not to give children worm expellers until the age of 2 years.

 Sunday Doctor, good morning to you. I recently did my annual health check, and they said my TSH is high. It was 6.2. I will share the results with you on WhatsApp. I am a 68-year-old woman going to 69. Everything else was normal, but they gave me Levothyroxin tablets. Whenever I take it, I don’t sleep because all my muscles just ache. I have stopped taking it on my own, even though I am due to see my GP next week. +1(301)******* 

Well, from what the results show, your TSH was even higher at 6.9 in 2025, and it reduced without treatment. As long as the other parameters of your thyroid function are normal, such as T3 and T4, you have no need to continue using this medication. But discuss this with your GP at your next appointment.

Sunday Doctor, Good day to you. I am a 40-year-old man with two children. I work in a bank and live in Lagos. For nearly one year now, I have not been getting erections. My wife and I are very disturbed. What is the solution now, please? 0803*******

The solution to the problem depends on the cause. You work in a Lagos bank, and knowing the working hours, stress may be a part of the problem. But you must first see a doctor for a proper examination, which will include tests, and then any associated problems will become obvious, and you can then get treated.

Sunday Doctor. I have been suffering from this constant headache for almost 1 month now. I have also done several tests for malaria and typhoid, but all were negative. My blood pressure is good. I don’t understand why the headache is there. What is your advice, sir? 0803*******

The problem may be with your eyes and the quality of your vision. You should get a proper eye test done to check for any kind of refractive errors. If you already use prescription glasses, perhaps the lens needs to be changed. Either way, get a proper test done. Unfortunately, you did not share your age or gender with us to enable us to offer a clearer piece of advice.

Sunday Doctor, my baby is now four months old. He had a swelling in the neck that you advised us to do physiotherapy for. I just want to appreciate this column and to say a big thank you, doctor. He can turn his neck well now, and the swelling has nearly disappeared. 0704*******

Well, thank you very much for the feedback. We appreciate that you followed the advice you were given, and congratulations on your baby’s progress.

Malaria remains Nigeria’s most urgent health issue, with cases resurging due to climate change, funding cuts, and drug resistance. Learn why it’s critical.

news.title: US to tell partners they must pick sides in AI race with China
news.text:
WASHINGTON – The US is preparing to tell dozens of countries they must pick sides in the artificial intelligence race with China, warning they will be excluded from a US-led AI coalition if they also sign up for Beijing’s competing framework, according to a US official and an internal draft reviewed by Reuters.

Washington in 2025 launched the Pax Silica initiative aimed at securing supply chains for AI models, semiconductors and critical minerals, amid a fierce technology rivalry with Beijing.

About two dozen countries have joined, including Kazakhstan, a key potential source of critical minerals that has also joined China’s coalition, as well as close US allies such as Japan, Australia and South Korea.

The draft letter, prepared by the State Department, is addressed to the 35 signatories of a US AI Opportunity Statement signed in June, which includes members of the non-binding Pax Silica framework and other countries that have expressed a desire to align cooperation on AI with Washington.

By pressing countries to choose sides, the US hopes to starve China of resources in a race to make the most sophisticated AI, which could be used for military or economic dominance.

In July, Chinese President ​Xi Jinping launched a rival World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, promoting his country’s open-weight technology as a challenge to US influence over ‌the fast-moving sector.

Kazakhstan is the only country so far known to have joined both initiatives, setting off alarm bells in Washington.

“To be part of everything is to be part of nothing. Signature of the Pax Silica Declaration is not merely a membership subscription, but a commitment,” the letter said, urging countries to “choose deliberately” on AI.

“It cannot be held alongside membership in duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with our own,” the letter said, without specifically mentioning China.

Reuters could not determine when the US intends to send the letter or whether it might be amended before sending.

The draft was undated. The State Department told Reuters it would not comment on “purportedly leaked internal documents”.

China’s embassy in Washington said the country opposes politicising trade and technology issues.

“Such actions will only stifle global AI advances and serve no one’s interests,” an embassy spokesperson said.

The Kazakh embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

‘Can’t have it both ways’

The Pax Silica agreement aims to push US allies and partners toward joint projects and export controls, and ultimately reduce reliance on adversaries for critical minerals, AI models and the semiconductor chips that power them.

The race between the US and China for technological leadership has reached a pivotal moment, as Chinese open-weight AI models have made rapid gains against proprietary systems from US companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

The exponential growth of the technology’s capabilities, including the ability to hack autonomously, has forced a global reckoning over its power.

Beijing is weighing restrictions on overseas access to some ​of China’s leading AI models, highlighting the growing tension with its stringent national security agenda.

The US touted Kazakhstan in June as the first country in Central Asia to join Pax Silica, bringing significant reserves of critical minerals that fuel advanced technologies.

China has used its current near-monopolies over critical minerals as a retaliatory weapon in a tariff war launched in 2025 by US President Donald Trump, who has ramped up US efforts to source the minerals domestically and from allies.

Members of Pax Silica have access to shared investment opportunities in AI-related projects while those who sign the AI Opportunity Statement have symbolically agreed on a “common purpose” and “shared vision” with the US, according to the statement posted on the State Department’s website.

US officials drafted the letter to make clear that “you can’t have it both ways”, the US official told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity given ongoing internal discussions on the issue.

“It’s difficult to see how a country can credibly position themselves as trusted partners in one technology ecosystem while simultaneously signing up for an initiative designed by China to advance a competing vision for AI,” the official said. REUTERS

news.title: Michael Goodwin: ‘Woke’ might be wounded — but the radical left is still infiltrating our politics
news.text:
The woke fever has broken, and the movement is wounded. But in the spirit of Mark Twain’s line that “reports of my death are greatly exaggerated,” ignore any claims that the mob of radical leftists rampaging through our politics has been defeated.

The impetus for the premature obituaries is a single race in Wisconsin where a wacky socialist squandered a huge lead and lost by a narrow margin to a more-centrist opponent in the Democrats’ primary for governor.

The oddities of the contest are too many to draw comforting conclusions from the outcome. They start with the fact that Francesca Hong, a member of the state assembly, lost by just 3,800 votes despite a history of calling for canceling Thanksgiving and defunding the police.

The victor, a black county executive named David Crowley, had dropped out of the race and then re-entered it. He had the support of just 7 percent in a late poll, but analysts say most undecided voters swung his way in the final days, giving him the nomination by less than half of a percentage point.

So hold the celebrations. Woke is wounded, but very much alive and still capable of doing more damage to America’s cohesion and leading gullible young minds into the weeds of society and the fantasies of revolution.

Like a contagious disease that turns its victims stark raving mad, it was born out of a hatred for Donald Trump after he had the nerve to defeat Hillary Clinton for the Oval Office in 2016.

Sen. Bernie Sanders ran far to the left of Clinton in the Dem primaries, but she controlled the party apparatus.

As the nominee, she played the dirtiest dirty trick ever with the fictional Steele dossier, and had no political heirs after her stunning defeat.

Instead, it was Sanders’ radical platform and energized youthful following that crowned him the godfather of woke.

His most durable and dynamic offspring is Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who pulled off a stunning upset in a 2018 congressional primary in Queens, and won the general election.

That might have been the apex of the movement, but it got a huge second wind with the George Floyd killing by Minneapolis police in May of 2020.

The burning, looting and murders that followed were widely excused by Dems and the media as legitimate responses, which helped to birth a movement for racial reparations and defunding police forces across the nation.

The opportunistic Black Lives Matter organization tapped white guilt for millions, but turned out to be mostly a fraud. That and the predictable crime surges following enforcement retreats and loony legal changes helped cool the anti-police fever.

Joe Biden’s presidency was inert, except for his insane open border policy and willingness to play footsie with crime and domestic radicals. His administration tried to racialize every dispute, but proved incompetent at that and in repairing the COVID-ravaged economy.

‘Moved away’

Trump’s comeback triumph in 2024 appeared to herald a fundamental shift to the right, but a year later, the leftists pulled off their biggest coup with the election of Zohran Mamdani as New York City’s mayor.

A Democratic Socialist who had embraced the defund the police mantra and the call to close all prisons, he added another sickening dimension to his tool kit: hating Israel.

He and Ocasio-Cortez, known everywhere as AOC, became the darlings of the movement and put New York in the vanguard of crazy.

Because reality offers a harsh education, Mamdani is having a tough time doing his first job and, as foreign born, is not eligible for the White House.

AOC is a different story: Senator, president — the world seemed to be hers for the taking.

And still could be because she appears to be growing up politically, and in other ways.

Her decision to go public with a video giving herself an injection in the process of freezing her eggs, suggests a new dimension to her public persona, along with the news that she and her boyfriend ended their engagement.

But for my money, the most significant revelation involves her latest views on what it means to be woke.

In an interview with ABC News, she said she and others had “moved away” from statements they made during the COVID madness, especially on cutting police budgets and closing prisons.

She quotes a city councilman as saying that, ‘Woke 1 was crazy’. . . especially during COVID.”

Looking back, she said, “I think that the doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place. And I actually think that the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful.”

Then she acknowledged a new reality: “When we talk about crime today, it’s fundamentally different than the way that we talked about crime . . . I think that we all share in the goals of having as low a crime rate as possible.”

She underscored the point by adding, “rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today.”

She’s not alone in coming to that realization. After James Talarico, a flaky Dem running for Senate in Texas, backed away from some of his weird history, a former Biden aide, Yemisi Egbewole, said on CNN that, “Peak woke got weird. It’s OK to say that!”

Mamdani, asked for his views on AOC’s comments, told reporters that “Sometimes what you believe in can change. I’ve made it very clear that I do not believe in defunding the police and I will not be defunding the police.”

Sounding like a conventional official of either party, he added that “to me, delivering critical public safety also looks like working with our police department alongside many other partners.”

He went on to cite record lows in murders and shootings on his watch, saying this “is how we measure public safety.”

Some who remain in the throes of revolution are very unhappy with AOC and Mamdani for moving away from their radical positions.

In a scorching essay, Guardian columnist Derecka Purnell warns that the two New Yorkers “backtracking on the defund movement puts organizers at risk.”

She essentially calls them sellouts who are too comfortable in their positions and doubts their sincerity in the first place. Writing that “Woke 1 represents a political baptism in shallow waters,” she says many people “were swept up in an emotional online conversion toward the radical, romantic rhetoric of defund the police.”

news.title: At least five reported dead amid flooding in US state of Indiana  - Puerto Rico Tribune – Daily Puerto Rico
news.text:
Authorities in the Midwestern United States have reported at least five deaths in Indiana after the state was struck with fierce storms and flooding.

Rescue workers continue to seek out those stranded by the storms, which drenched Indiana over the past week.

Governor Mike Braun had called for a presidential emergency declaration on Friday, in order to access greater resources for the state.

On Saturday, he issued a public statement announcing that the federal government had pledged assistance.

“I spoke with President [Donald] Trump today about the severe storms and historic flooding impacting Indiana, and he informed me that he intends to approve our request for a Presidential Emergency Declaration,” Braun, a Republican, wrote in a social media post.

Emergency workers have used boats to rescue people from homes inundated by rising waters.

The White River in Indianapolis, Indiana, was among the waterways that overflowed its banks over the last week, causing dangerous flooding.

news.title: Trump-linked crypto venture World Liberty Trust granted bank status in unprecedented move for president
news.text:
A Trump-appointed national bank regulator granted a wing of the Trump family's crypto business conditional approval to establish a bank charter, opening the door for larger clients and potentially heightened profits.

The decision marks the first time in U.S. history that a company owned by the sitting president's family has been granted bank status, as Democratic lawmakers express concerns over potential conflicts of interest.

In a letter published Friday, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted World Liberty Trust Co., an organization that is 38% owned by "an entity affiliated with Donald J. Trump and certain of his family members," according to its website, the ability to issue stablecoin cryptocurrency tied to the U.S. dollar.

World Liberty Financial, the listed sponsor of the conditionally approved trust, has previously relied on a third-party crypto company, BitGo, to provide a stable digital currency. Friday's approval allows the Trump family's business to cut out the middleman and provide the service directly. 

Digital currencies, like Bitcoin, are historically volatile and therefore less appealing for entities making large transactions.

Crypto tied to more stable values, like the U.S. dollar or the price of gold, can be more attractive to big spenders and can be "marketed for use as a means of making payments, transmitting money, or storing value," according to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

The decision allows the Trump-linked business to act as a bank, issuing digital currency to clients for transactions. Clients would exchange the U.S. dollar for the stablecoin, with profits going directly to the Trump family's crypto business. 

The president's family has seen extensive profit from World Liberty Financial, securing around $5 billion in the company's first days after going public, according to the token's value at the time, with major investments from individuals and foreign nations continuing to fuel the company's value.

Trump himself has made more than $1.4 billion in business revenue from his family's crypto ventures, according to his released financial disclosures. 

White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly has maintained that the president "only acts in the best interests of the American public," and said that no conflict of interest exists in part because the president's assets are held in a blind trust managed by his children. Typically, a blind trust would operate with an independent trustee.

"President Trump’s assets are in a trust managed by his children," Kelly said. "There are no conflicts of interest."

State-backed Abu Dhabi investment firm MGX invested another $2 billion in the company in May 2025, promising to use the Trump family's USD1 stablecoin in large transactions with crypto exchange company Binance.

The deal later came under scrutiny when the Trump administration then agreed to supply the UAE with highly coveted American-made AI chips despite prior administration concerns that they may make their way to China.

"We thank MGX and Binance for their trust in us, and I think it's only the beginning," World Liberty Financial co-founder Zach Witkoff said after announcing the deal, alongside the president's son Eric Trump at a crypto convention in Dubai.

Witkoff is the son of the president's special envoy to the Middle East, Steve Witkoff.

Ranking Member of the Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., urged the OCC to halt approval of Trump-linked business ventures, writing a letter to the comptroller in January. As an executive branch office, the president has ultimate authority over the OCC, though the office considers itself independent.

"For the first time in history, the president of the United States would be in charge of overseeing his own financial company," Warren wrote.

Following the OCC's preliminary approval, Warren described the decision as the "most brazen act of self-dealing our financial system has ever seen."

"I’m introducing a bill to stop this kind of unprecedented corruption," Warren said in a post on social media.

"The Comptroller and staff acted consistently with their statutory duties and ethical obligations with respect to the Application," the OCC wrote Friday. "OCC staff reviewed this Application in accordance with the agency’s established policies and procedures."

The charter application will not be fully approved until some conditions are met, including increasing the company's capital, the OCC said.
news.summary: A national bank regulator granted a wing of the Trump family's crypto business conditional approval to establish a bank charter, opening the door for larger clients.

news.title: Colombia leader asks Trump to suspend tariffs after deadly quake
news.text:
Colombia’s new President Abelardo de la Espriella on Saturday called on his US counterpart Donald Trump to suspend tariffs currently targeting the South American nation, which is reeling after a deadly earthquake.
US tariffs on Colombian products rose from 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent in late July, with a few exceptions including coffee and oil.
“I asked him to consider to temporarily suspend the high tariffs that are affecting Colombian products, in order to give some relief to our business owners, who are facing very difficult times due to the effects of the earthquake,” De la Espriella said on social media.
The increased tariffs went into effect on July 24, replacing an expiring global duty rolled out by Trump earlier this year.
De la Espriella said he has spoken for about 10 minutes with Trump, who expressed his condolences over the deaths from Monday’s 7.4-magnitude quake.

“The conversation was very friendly and cordial,” the Colombian leader said.
“I told him that we have a huge challenge ahead: rebuilding Colombia amid the extremely difficult and apocalyptic economic situation that I inherited.”
The tremor devastated the western Colombian cities of Cali and Pereira, leaving nearly 300 people dead and destroying almost 13,000 homes.
Trump endorsed the right-wing De la Espriella, a millionaire lawyer-turned-politician, during his run for the presidency.
Since taking office, De la Espriella – who succeeded the leftist Gustavo Petro – has joined the so-called “Shield of the Americas,” an anti-cartel alliance headed by Trump and made up of pro-US governments across Latin America, including Argentina, Ecuador and El Salvador.
Member states exchange information and coordinate judicial and security forces to address transnational criminal activity.
De la Espriella plans to forge a military alliance with the US and Israel to help bolster his war on guerrillas.

news.title: Woke Bay Area school took children on trip to mosque where girls were 'encouraged' to hear HIJABS while being told that Islam is aligned with social justice: lawsuit
news.text:
A group of Bay Area parents and students are suing their local school district over a 2025 field trip where children were allegedly encouraged to wear Muslim religious attire like hijabs while visiting a mosque.

The federal suit filed last week by ten Palo Alto High School students names the Palo Alto Unified School District and Principal Brent Kline as defendants.

It alleges that photographs of the students were also posted online, without the parents' permission.

Students were also 'exposed' to 'a controversial speaker known for publicly documented hostile and discriminatory statements regarding Jews and sharply ideological political views' known as Zahra Billoo, according to the suit.

Billoo, the executive director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), was 'allowed unfettered access to students to advocate personal religious and political views without balancing perspective or adequate supervision,' it alleged. 

Billoo, a civil rights lawyer who said Donald Trump was 'going to do to you Muslims what Hitler did to the Jews' after he was reelected, told The San Francisco Chronicle this week that any 'exposure' to her was merely educational.

She said she only imparted her experiences as an American Muslim woman working in civil rights and social justice. The suit argues students were told that the tenets of Islam aligned with social justice work.

The plaintiffs are two Jewish parents of Palo Alto High students, three former Jewish students, a Hindu parent and another Zoroastrian. Four others are anonymous.

The trip was to the Muslim Community Association’s mosque in Santa Clara this past fall. It was part of a three-year program at the school that focused on addressing social problems.

The lawsuit maintains it was a 'coercive school-sponsored religious activity' that violated laws limiting partisan or biased advocacy in public schools. 

'Public schools and the government have an obligation to remain neutral toward religion, but what neutrality does not mean is shielding students entirely,' Billoo told the Chronicle.

'The job of educators is to teach students, and expose them to different worldviews. That’s what happened here.'

She added that she was 'concerned that this group of parents not only wants to counteract that for their own children… but is attempting to intimidate schools and school districts from doing necessary work of educating the next generation.'

Photos posted to the Muslim Community Association's Facebook page, meanwhile, show her speaking to Palo Alto High School students back in November. It's unclear if the photos show the trip specifically mentioned in the lawsuit.

Parents are now seeking monetary damages, as well as an admission from the school district that it was negligent in supervising students and violated their and parents' privacy rights. 

Palo Alto Unified School District Superintendent Jason Glass told the Chronicle Friday that the district only found out about the suit through news coverage. He said that he had yet to personally read the complaint.

He said the district had not yet been served with the court papers.

Glass could not yet verify the allegations.
news.summary: The federal suit alleges that photographs of the students were also posted online, without the parents' permission.

news.title: US to tell partners they must pick sides in AI race with China
news.text:
The US launched the Pax Silica initiative to secure supply chains for AI models, semiconductors and critical minerals amid a fierce technology rivalry with China. (AFP pic)
WASHINGTON: The US is preparing to tell dozens of countries they must pick sides in the artificial intelligence (AI) race with China, warning they will be excluded from a US-led AI coalition if they also sign up for Beijing's competing framework, according to a US official and an internal draft reviewed by Reuters.
Washington last year launched the Pax Silica initiative aimed at securing supply chains for AI models, semiconductors and critical minerals, amid a fierce technology rivalry with Beijing.
About two dozen countries have joined, including Kazakhstan, a key potential source of critical minerals that has also joined China's coalition, as well as close US allies such as Japan, Australia and South Korea.
The draft letter, prepared by the state department, is addressed to the 35 signatories of a US "AI Opportunity Statement" signed in June, which includes members of the non-binding Pax Silica framework and other countries that have expressed a desire to align cooperation on AI with Washington.
By pressing countries to choose sides the US hopes to starve China of resources in a race to make the most sophisticated AI, which could be used for military or economic dominance.
In July, Chinese president ​Xi Jinping launched a rival "World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization", promoting his country's open-weight technology as a challenge to US influence over ‌the fast-moving sector.
Kazakhstan is the only country so far known to have joined both initiatives, setting off alarm bells in Washington.
"To be part of everything is to be part of nothing. Signature of the Pax Silica Declaration is not merely a membership subscription, but a commitment," the letter says, urging countries to "choose deliberately" on AI.
"It cannot be held alongside membership in duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with our own," the letter said, without specifically mentioning China.
Reuters could not determine when the US intends to send the letter or whether it might be amended before sending. The draft was undated.
The state department told Reuters it would not comment on "purportedly leaked internal documents".
China’s embassy in Washington said the country opposes politicising trade and technology issues. 
“Such actions will only stifle global AI advances and serve no one’s interests,” an embassy spokesman said.
The Kazakh embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.
'Can't have it both ways'
The Pax Silica agreement aims to push US allies and partners toward joint projects and export controls, and ultimately reduce reliance on adversaries for critical minerals, AI models and the semiconductor chips that power them.
The race between the US and China for technological leadership has reached a pivotal moment, as Chinese open-weight AI models have made rapid gains against proprietary systems from US companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
The exponential growth of the technology's capabilities, including the ability to hack autonomously, has forced a global reckoning over its power.
Beijing is weighing restrictions on overseas access to some ​of China's leading AI models, highlighting the growing tension with its stringent national security agenda.
The US touted Kazakhstan in June as the first country in Central Asia to join Pax Silica, bringing significant reserves of critical minerals that fuel advanced technologies.
China has used its current near-monopolies over critical minerals as a retaliatory weapon in a tariff war launched last year by US president Donald Trump, who has ramped up US efforts to source the minerals domestically and from allies.
Members of Pax Silica have access to shared investment opportunities in AI-related projects while those who sign the AI Opportunity Statement have symbolically agreed on a "common purpose" and "shared vision" with the US, according to the statement posted on the state department's website.
US officials drafted the letter to make clear that "you can't have it both ways," the US official told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity given ongoing internal discussions on the issue.
"It's difficult to see how a country can credibly position itself as trusted partners in one technology ecosystem while simultaneously signing up for an initiative designed by China to advance a competing vision for AI," the official said.
news.summary: The US warns countries they could be excluded from its AI coalition if they sign up for Beijing’s competing framework.
news.author: Reuters

news.title: US Troops Can Make Arrests in Militarized Border Zones, DOJ Says
news.text:
U.S. troops deployed at designated border defense zones should have the authority to make arrests, according to an advisory opinion authored by the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel and published on Aug. 14.

Though a U.S. law known as the Posse Comitatus Act generally prohibits federal U.S. troops from engaging in domestic law enforcement activities, President Donald Trump has increasingly called on the military to help secure the border and disrupt illegal crossing attempts.

The new opinion from the Justice Department concludes that U.S. troops would not violate the Posse Comitatus Act by arresting individuals suspected of committing offenses in a designated National Defense Area.

Last year, Trump issued a presidential memorandum that called for the establishment of National Defense Areas along the border. Since then, the U.S. government has designated six of these zones along sections of the border in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas.

“Our Office and the courts have consistently recognized that the [Posse Comitatus Act] ‘does not prohibit military involvement in actions that are primarily military or foreign affairs related, even if they have an incidental effect on law enforcement, provided that such actions are not undertaken for the purpose of executing the laws,’” the Office of Legal Counsel said.

The Office of Legal Counsel also noted that commanders of U.S. military bases have historically held the authority to maintain law and order on those bases, including by stopping outside trespassers.

Further, the Office of Legal Counsel assessed that U.S. troops on military installations may arrest individuals “just outside” a military installation for violations that occurred on said installation.

Under federal law, trespassing on a military installation is a misdemeanor offense punishable by up to six months in prison and a $500 fine. Violating defense property security regulations is a misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in prison and a $100,000 fine.

The American Civil Liberties Union has shared concerns that these National Defense Areas—some of which cover open terrain with no standing structures—are not well-marked, raising the possibility of accidental trespassing, including by U.S. citizens living in the vicinity.
news.summary: The Posse Comitatus Act generally prohibits federal U.S. troops from engaging in domestic law enforcement activities, albeit with some exceptions.
news.author: Ryan Morgan
